# Submission name:

`semantic-pose-HPAC_CPR1_polished`

Repo with full experimental setup and results: https://github.com/codexblack/CommaVideoCompressionChallenge_ExperimentBook

# Upload zipped `archive.zip`

[archive.zip](https://github.com/codexblack/comma_video_compression_challenge/releases/download/semantic-pose-HPAC_CPR1_polished-f26/archive.zip)

SHA-256: `12cf5d71a94065184f097c3e40dfe9f1db8402a1a76a80efc76a6956fe1e4004`

Size: `186,724` bytes

The archive contains one stored ZIP member, `p` (`186,624` bytes).

# report.txt

```
=== Evaluation results over 600 samples ===
  Average PoseNet Distortion: 0.00000688
  Average SegNet Distortion: 0.00029639
  Submission file size: 186,724 bytes
  Original uncompressed size: 37,545,489 bytes
  Compression Rate: 0.00497327
  Final score: 100*segnet_dist + √(10*posenet_dist) + 25*rate = 0.16
```

Byte exact score was reported as `0.16226842169958583`.

# Does your submission require gpu for evaluation (inflation)?

Yes. Use the T4 GPU.

# Did you include the compression script? and want it to be merged?

Yes. `compress.sh` is included for reproducible archive preparation and is intended to be merged. The exploratory training and search pipeline remains in the separate frozen experiment repository and is not part of this submission.

# Is this submission competitive or innovative? explain why

The submission is competitive, beating both the current leaderboard topper (semantic-pose-HPAC_CPR1: score 0.172) and the not-yet-merged #133 (unofficial score: 0.166).
We managed to remove around ~4.3KB from the archive size (using the leaderboard topper as a baseline for our solution), mostly by stacking together small, lossless changes in many areas. Combined with the findings in #133 (~3.5KB improvement in comparison), which we were independently exploring before deciding to adapt the existing results already, we were able to enjoy such gains while having our PoseNet and SegNet distortion improve as well.

While we don't show any real innovation, stacking simple ideas have allowed us to achieve non-negligible improvements over both #130 and #133 in raw score and archive size.

| Candidate | Raw bytes | PoseNet | SegNet | Archive size | Score |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| PR 130 | 37,545,489 | 0.0000233100 | 0.000296600 | 191,052 | 0.17† |
| PR 133 | 37,545,489 | 0.00000896000 | 0.000296600 | 190,212 | 0.165780 |
| Ours | 37,545,489 | 0.00000688439 | 0.000296394 | 186,724 | 0.162268 |

† PR 130's official evaluator published the score rounded to two digits, the raw scores showed great variation among those who ran it

# Additional comments

We build upon #133's int12 coefficient polishing idea by using a Jacobian-guided discrete carrier search to resolve the coefficients, further improving PoseNet distortion over that solution. Frame-0 edits are also helpful to improve PoseNet further with no impact on SegNet. We used a selector with K=8 (our best out of 16, 8, 4) where K is the number of fixed ways from which we can modify Frame 0, choosing the option that reduces distortion the most. This added 236 bytes to the archive. To reduce that we baked the selections directly into the int12 co-efficient rows, nullifying the size.

Making changes to the renderer to improve SegNet can cause a regression in the PoseNet scores. The exact renderer screen evaluated candidate moves over all 600 pairs of frames using both SegNet and PoseNet. These two FiLM (Feature-wise Linear Modulation) edits improved SegNet, but initially regressed PoseNet.
We then froze the renderer edits and  frame-0 selector, and re-solved the frame-0 carrier. The final carrier search tested all 24 singleton ±1 moves across the 12 int12 dimensions for each identity-selector row, accepting only exact PoseNet improvements. It changed 473 carrier rows and 2,234 int12 symbols.
Those carrier changes affect frame 0, so they recover PoseNet without undoing the SegNet benefit from the frame-1 FiLM edits. The SegNet distortion improvement was 1.0171788744628429e-7, contributing 1.0171788744628429e-5 to the total score reduction.

For lossless compression, we used the following techniques:
- **Fixed Schema Container:** The archive now derives fixed shapes, section lengths, versions, and boundaries from the decoder schema instead of storing them repeatedly. We also searched raw-LZMA2 settings and field order, along with tightening canonical HPAC rows. This saved us around 328 bytes.
- **WANS1 semantic renderer representation:** WANS1 entropy-codes the fixed renderer streams independently while keeping the decoded tensors unchanged, saving 610 bytes.
- **CAP1 carrier representation:** CAP1 stores the carrier basis, coefficient scales, predictor metadata, and int12 residuals using exact AR/Rice coding. We see a reduction of 81 bytes.
- **RC64 token stream:** We replaced the previous token coder with a 63-bit streaming arithmetic coder. It converts each five-class float32 probability row into shared, deterministic integer frequencies totaling 2^31. One of the largest savings at 2,122 bytes dropped.
- **Carrier basis reductions:** Three basis atoms were reduced from five bits to four bits to save 815 bytes (PR #133 is the source for this).

#### Unsuccessful ideas

- **Sub 4-bit quantization**: Exploring 3 bit quant (both PQT and QAT) for some layers resulted in size reductions, but with huge amounts of PoseNet and SegNet regression.
- **HPAC LoRA**: The HPAC model predicts the token stream that is later arithmetic-coded. The idea was to add a very small low-rank weight update instead of rewriting the large HPAC model. Ultimately across all our combinations, it did not recover its cost.
- **Alternative Pose Generators**: We try to replace the carrier with a more lightweight structured generator. However the frame-1 derived bases lacked enough pose information to be useful.

### Lineage

The direct artifact lineage is:

- [PR #130](https://github.com/commaai/comma_video_compression_challenge/pull/130) for CPR1 and its documented [semantic-pose/HPAC lineage](https://github.com/fesalfayed/comma-ai-semantic-pose-hpac-cpr1/blob/semantic-pose-HPAC_CPR1/LINEAGE_AND_CITATIONS.md);
- [PR #133](https://github.com/commaai/comma_video_compression_challenge/pull/133) for CBQ and the complete re-solved int12 carrier.

Inherited architectural prior work includes:

- jas0xf’s semantic-token renderer, HPAC path, and asymmetric frame roles in [PR #86](https://github.com/commaai/comma_video_compression_challenge/pull/86);
- EthanYangTW’s pose-conditioned generation and low-rank spatial actuation in [PR #67](https://github.com/commaai/comma_video_compression_challenge/pull/67) and [PR #79](https://github.com/commaai/comma_video_compression_challenge/pull/79).

The following PRs were used for ideas:

- avocardio’s [PR #64](https://github.com/commaai/comma_video_compression_challenge/pull/64) for consolidating related streams;
- celikemir’s [PR #73](https://github.com/commaai/comma_video_compression_challenge/pull/73) for fixed-schema flat packing and stream-order searches;
- adpena’s [PR #110](https://github.com/commaai/comma_video_compression_challenge/pull/110) for exploiting the evaluator’s asymmetric frame roles with a per-pair frame-0 selector;
- mattneel’s [PR #112](https://github.com/commaai/comma_video_compression_challenge/pull/112) for losslessly re-coding frozen learned state;
- Bucky789’s [PR #125](https://github.com/commaai/comma_video_compression_challenge/pull/125), ryanli0070’s [PR #127](https://github.com/commaai/comma_video_compression_challenge/pull/127), and a12dongithub’s [PR #128](https://github.com/commaai/comma_video_compression_challenge/pull/128) for quantization-aware, exact-grid, and exact-score-gated discrete polishing.

### LLM coding-agent setup

Codex with GPT-5.6 was used as a research and implementation assistant, not as the source of truth for results. It searched the repository, edited project code, ran bounded experiments, built archives, and wrote reports. Every technical claim had to be backed by a reproducible artifact or evaluator output.

I used deep research to help gather related documents to familiarize myself with the State of the Art in this type of work, then designed experiments around ideas I thought may be worth considering.

The agent ran in the project workspace with:

- Windows PowerShell
- Isolated Python 3.11 environments
- CPU and CUDA environments
- `rg` for source and report inspection
- `apply_patch` for code changes
- The project’s existing archive, inflation, and evaluation scripts

The PR #130 archive was the fixed baseline. Frozen challenge and CPR1 checkouts, model weights, token sources, and evaluator inputs were not modified.

Each experiment followed the same loop:

1. State the baseline archive bytes, SHA-256, decoded-state hashes, and score.
2. Make one bounded change.
3. Rebuild the complete archive twice.
4. Require byte-identical repeated builds.
5. Inflate the archive and verify semantic, carrier, residual, and token parity.
6. Run the full 600-pair evaluator.
7. Keep the change only if the charged archive and full score improved.

The agent was instructed to distinguish:

- Proxy or cached metrics from full evaluator results
- Raw component savings from complete archive savings
- Lossless representation changes from changes to decoded model state
- SegNet, PoseNet, and rate effects
- Screening candidates from promoted candidates

A typical task prompt was:

```text
Start from this exact baseline archive and SHA-256.

Change only these files or functions.
Preserve these decoded-state and token hashes.
Build and charge the complete archive.
Reject the change if either the repeated archive, inflation parity,
or full 600-pair score gate fails.

Report:
- files changed
- exact algorithm
- archive bytes and SHA-256
- PoseNet and SegNet distortion
- rate and final score
- comparison with baseline
- rejected alternatives
```

The final decision always came from deterministic archive construction, fresh inflation, and the pinned full evaluator.

Thanks for the submission @codexblack! 🤏

A maintainer will review your PR shortly.

To run the evaluation, a maintainer will trigger the `eval` workflow with your PR number.

I am also looking for full-time Software Engineer or Machine Learning Engineer roles. I have a Bachelors and Masters degree in Computer Science (AI concentration) with 2 years of professional experience.

> see https://github.com/commaai/comma_video_compression_challenge/blob/master/README.md#coding-agents-and-llms-policy

I respect your decision, but I have to say I find it really odd considering some of the current winners sniped the actual winning idea (conceptually), with very marginal improvements. I don't see any evidence they are really "hand written" either. 300ish lines and they score pretty much the same.

But just because I wanted to run more ablations on ideas I had (without having to manually watch through it all and gate it, which is like watching paint dry) instead of just stopping at removing a few hundred bytes through a few tricks somehow makes it "worse"?

I fail to see how I have put in "less" human work than some of the winners of the cash prize.

This is a new policy. Also you’re welcome to re-open this PR with a real description. What were the ideas you had? Which ones worked? 
If you expect your PR to be reviewed by a human, you have to show that there was some human work.

> This is a new policy

Oh, in that case it makes a lot more sense. There are many more details on the README of the repo where I actually conducted the experiments (linked at the top: https://github.com/codexblack/CommaVideoCompressionChallenge_ExperimentBook), I was not sure of how much to add to the PR itself, considering most submissions weren't very verbose.
If the inauthentic description is the ONLY issue with this submission, I would be happy to re-do it and include more details about what I have done. If there are other concerns, please let me know because I don't want to spam this repo with ineligible PRs.

> If you expect your PR to be reviewed by a human, you have to show that there was some human work.

Touché. Mainly was just curious why this policy did not seem to apply to some other solutions, which is now explained to me. I don't really disagree with it, as a whole.

We don’t need more verbose, we need more precise. The description should read: 
- **THIS** is the baseline submission and score… 
- **THIS** file/function/etc was changed to do **THIS** instead and achieved score…
- Optionally: **THIS** didn’t work better…
- Optionally: **THIS** is my llm setup and prompts…

> We don’t need more verbose, we need more precise. The description should read:
> 
> * **THIS** is the baseline submission and score…
> * **THIS** file/function/etc was changed to do **THIS** instead and achieved score…
> * Optionally: **THIS** didn’t work better…
> * Optionally: **THIS** is my llm setup and prompts…

I have updated the description to touch upon these points. It was written manually, apart from the lineage part which I kept from the previous version. If it looks acceptable I would like to re-open this PR.

Also, thank you for taking the time to point me in the right direction! I had initially assumed the whole submission was ineligible, not just the description
Does this mean I am allowed to use this to apply for a full-time role, or does this not qualify since it is not innovative enough?
